title: Tactical seller summaries for hyperscaler RFP answers
content:
Purpose:
Quick, copy-ready snippets and short-answer templates sellers and solutions engineers can drop into RFPs, procurement decks, and security reviews when the buyer is comparing hyperscaler managed endpoints (AWS/GCP/Azure) to Redwood Inference. This is intentionally tactical - usable verbatim with minimal editing.

Audience:
Sales reps, solutions engineers, customer engineering, deal desk. Assumes technical buyer/architect reviewing operational, cost, and compliance tradeoffs.

TL;DR bullets (ready to paste):
- Redwood focuses on production inference economics: we optimize for predictable per-request latency and per-token cost across hosted, dedicated and private deployments (not single-cloud managed endpoints).
- We provide native fallbacks, model variants, and policy routing so your application stays available even when a single endpoint is saturated.
- If you need private networking, on-premise options, or customer-managed keys with audit trails, Redwood supports these without losing the operational tooling of a hosted service.
- Typical customers see 20-40% unit-cost reduction through smart batching, prefix caching and quantization guidance vs naive managed endpoints, and convert that into higher throughput or lower AWS/GCP spend.

Competitive signals to address early (what buyers will assume):
- "Hyperscalers will be cheaper because of scale." -> Counter: raw VM/GPU cost is only one axis; inference economics are dominated by cache hit rates, batching efficiency, model quantization and fallback logic. Redwood measures and tunes the full stack for per-query cost under realistic tail-latency SLOs.
- "Managed endpoints solve reliability for me." -> Counter: hyperscaler endpoints give isolation but limited routing/fallback and limited transparent per-route diagnostics. Redwood provides policy routing, automatic compatible-fallbacks, and token-level tracing so you can reason about failures and cost per feature.
- "Vendor lock-in to hyperscalers is low risk." -> Counter: lock-in often surfaces in operational playbooks, networking, and data controls. Redwood's same API across hosted/dedicated/private reduces migration risk and avoids re-architecting app logic when you change infrastructure.

One-paragraph boilerplate you can paste into decks or RFP responses:
Redwood Inference is a developer-first inference platform that combines a GPU-optimized serving runtime with a control plane for rollout, observability, and failover. Unlike hyperscaler managed endpoints, Redwood lets teams choose deployment mode (hosted API, dedicated reserved capacity, or private VPC/on-prem) while keeping a consistent API, transparent per-token cost visibility, and built-in operational fallbacks. This reduces end-to-end inference cost, improves tail latency predictability, and accelerates migrations between clouds without application rewrites.

Top RFP Q&A templates (short answers + optional expanded talking points):
1) Q: How do you guarantee latency and availability?
   Short: We provide per-route latency SLOs on Dedicated and SLAs on Enterprise plans; the runtime uses dynamic batching, KV/prefix caching and smart routing with fallback tiers for availability.
   Expand: Explain autoscaling behavior, how KV cache warmup works, typical cold-start numbers, and canaries for rollouts. Point to latency dashboards and a sample SLO table.

2) Q: How does pricing compare to hyperscaler endpoints?
   Short: We price for consumed inference units (tokens/embeddings) plus optional reserved capacity. Typical unit cost is lower after accounting for batching and cache gains; customers often reallocate savings to higher concurrency or quality variants.
   Expand: Provide example math (tokens per second, cache hit rate assumptions, GPU-hour cost). Offer a modeling worksheet as attachment.

3) Q: Can you operate in our VPC and integrate with our KMS/HSM?
   Short: Yes - Redwood Private supports deployment into customer VPCs and integrates with common KMS solutions; on-prem options support HSMs via our enterprise package.
   Expand: Attach network topology diagram, checklist of supported KMS vendors, and audit log examples.

4) Q: How do you handle model rollouts and regressions?
   Short: We support canary rollouts, A/B experiments, automatic fallback policies and prompt-set-based regression alerts.
   Expand: Describe evaluation hooks, metric surfaces we track (per-prompt accuracy, latency, token consumption), and example rollback scenarios.

5) Q: What security certifications or controls do you offer?
   Short: Redwood supports SOC2 controls, role-based access, audit logs, and tenant isolation; Private customers can meet stricter compliance via on-prem deployment.
   Expand: Link to security page and list of compliance artifacts available under NDA.

Objection handling (short snappy lines to use on calls):
- "We already run on X cloud." -> "Great - Redwood plays well with your cloud, and our routing layer can spill over to public endpoints or dedicated pools while keeping the same API. Think of us as operational consistency, not cloud replacement"
- "Hyperscaler is simpler." -> "Simplicity at first glance often costs you in tail latency, debugging, and migration. We remove those operational surprises with per-route visibility and fallbacks"
- "We can build this ourselves." -> "Building a production-grade inference stack is an order of magnitude more effort - caching, kernel selection, autoscaling, latency SLOs and robust rollouts are all subtle. We give you that as an out-of-the-box product with engineering support"

Demo hooks / technical call checklist (what SE should show):
- Live trace showing a burst of requests, cache hits/misses and resulting latency distribution.
- Canary rollout: swap a model variant for 5% traffic and show automatic rollback on a regression signal.
- Private deployment snippet: show a VPC peering diagram and KMS configuration YAML.
- Cost model worksheet: 2 scenarios (hyperscaler managed endpoint baseline vs Redwood with caching/batching).

Metrics and artifacts buyers ask for (how to answer quickly):
- P95 latency numbers by model family and sequence length (give table or link to benchmark).
- Typical cache hit rates and effect on tokens per second.
- Example customer case: ecommerce search reranker that cut inference cost 28% while reducing 99th percentile latency by 45%.

Red flags / signals the buyer really cares about (call them out early):
- Networking regime: VPC peering, egress costs, and transit path requirements.
- Data residency and auditability requirements.
- Plateau tolerance: whether the buyer expects zero-impact scale to 10k qps or needs staging/burst plans.

Suggested play for deals > $250k ARR:
- Offer a 6-8 week pilot with a scoped POC: model onboarding, cost baseline, and 2 production routes instrumented for regressions. Include pricing credits for engineering time and a documented success criteria checklist.

Next steps / action items for seller: (one-line)
- Attach benchmark artifact and cost worksheet to RFP.
- Book technical deep-dive with SE if buyer lists "latency" or "SLA" as critical.
- Propose pilot when buyer indicates multi-cloud, VPC, or migration concerns.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Update attached benchmark links after privacy review (CONFLUENCE-1234).
- Get fresh cost worksheet from finance (JIRA-RT-987).
- Pull legal template for Private KMS onboarding.

End.
